lead: Cruise control keeps a car at a speed the driver chooses, without the driver holding the pedal. It measures actual speed, compares it with the set speed, and moves the throttle through a controller. Adaptive cruise control (ACC) adds a forward sensor: it also measures the gap to the car ahead and slows or brakes to keep a safe time gap. Used on highways, in stop-and-go traffic, and in many new cars sold in India with radar or camera systems.
prereq: You need Unit 4 for how throttle changes engine torque, Unit 3 for radar and speed sensors, and 5.1 for how a controller commands an actuator.

blocks.text: Basic cruise control holds a driver-chosen speed. The driver presses SET above a minimum speed, often around 30 km/h. The controller stores the set speed v_set. RESUME brings back the stored speed after a cancel. CANCEL or a tap on the brake ends control. COAST lowers the stored speed without using the pedal. Actual speed v comes from wheel speed sensors.
e = v_set − v;   u = Kp·e + Ki·∫e dt
blocks.where: e is speed error in m/s; v_set is set speed in m/s; v is actual speed in m/s; u is throttle command (0 to 100 %); Kp is proportional gain; Ki is integral gain; t is time in s.

blocks.text: The P term gives an immediate response. The I term sums error over time. On a hill, a plain P controller leaves a steady error: uphill needs more throttle, and the only way a P controller makes more throttle is to keep a positive error. The integral keeps adding while error exists, until error returns to zero. On downhill, the integral unwinds. If the car still goes faster than set, basic cruise cannot brake; it has throttle authority only.

ACC adds a forward sensor, usually a 77 GHz radar or a camera, and a gap loop. Radar measures distance d in metres to the lead car and relative speed. Target selection picks the nearest car in the host lane with the smallest time gap; the camera helps identify lanes.
t_gap = d ÷ v;   d_target = t_target × v;   e_gap = d − d_target;   closing rate = v − v_lead
blocks.where: t_gap is time gap in s; d is measured distance to lead car in m; v is host speed in m/s; t_target is selected time gap in s; d_target is desired distance in m; e_gap is gap error in m; v_lead is lead car speed in m/s.

blocks.text: Time gap is in seconds, not metres. The driver selects t_target, often 1.5 to 2.5 s. At a higher speed the same time gap needs a larger distance, so d_target grows with v. A positive e_gap means the host is farther than target; a negative e_gap means it is closer and must slow. Closing rate is positive when the gap is shrinking.

The controller combines speed error and gap error. If the gap is large, it follows set speed. As the gap falls, it reduces speed; if needed it applies the service brakes through ESP (5.4). Basic cruise has no brake authority. A car cutting in makes d drop suddenly; the controller brakes, but if the cut-in is too close the driver must brake. Stop-and-go ACC can brake to zero and restart. The brake pedal always cancels or overrides; the accelerator can also override. Radar processing is in 5.8; PI tuning is in 5.9.

examples.question: A host car is set to 25 m/s. Its 77 GHz radar sees a lead car in the same lane travelling at 20 m/s at a distance of 60 m. The driver has selected a 2.0 s time gap. (a) Find the present time gap. (b) Find the target distance. (c) Find the gap error. (d) Find the closing rate. (e) At the present speeds, how long before the gap would become zero if nothing changed? (f) What average deceleration removes the 5 m/s closing speed over that time?
steps: Present time gap: t_gap = d ÷ v_host = 60 m ÷ 25 m/s = 2.4 s.
Target distance: d_target = t_target × v_host = 2.0 s × 25 m/s = 50 m.
Gap error: e_gap = d − d_target = 60 m − 50 m = +10 m. The host is 10 m farther than target.
Closing rate: v_host − v_lead = 25 m/s − 20 m/s = 5 m/s. Positive, so the gap is shrinking.
Time to zero gap at present speeds: t = d ÷ closing rate = 60 m ÷ 5 m/s = 12 s. The target gap itself is reached earlier, in (60 − 50) ÷ 5 = 2 s.
Average deceleration: a = closing rate ÷ t = 5 m/s ÷ 12 s = 0.4167 ≈ 0.42 m/s².
examples.answer: The time gap is 2.4 s, target distance 50 m, gap error +10 m, closing rate 5 m/s, time to zero gap 12 s, and average deceleration 0.42 m/s².
examples.check:
v_host = 25
v_lead = 20
d = 60
t_target = 2.0
t_gap = d / v_host
d_target = t_target * v_host
e_gap = d - d_target
closing = v_host - v_lead
t_zero = d / closing
a = closing / t_zero
print(round(t_gap, 1))
print(round(d_target))
print(round(e_gap))
print(round(closing))
print(round(t_zero))
print(round(a, 2))

traps: Basic cruise control cannot brake; it only moves the throttle. On a long downhill the car can exceed set speed.
Time gap is in seconds, not metres. The target distance changes with speed: 2.0 s is 50 m at 25 m/s but 40 m at 20 m/s.
Set speed is not actual speed while the loop is catching up. The error is v_set − v, not v_set alone.
Gap error sign matters. Positive e_gap means the host is farther than target, not closer.
The brake pedal always overrides ACC. ACC brake force comes through the service brakes and ESP, not from a separate pedal.

quiz.q: What does the SET button store in basic cruise control?
quiz.a: It stores the current speed as v_set, the set speed.

quiz.q: Name two forward sensors used by ACC.
Why does a PI controller need the integral term to hold speed on a hill?
quiz.a: A P controller needs a steady error to make extra throttle. Uphill, that leaves the car slower than set. The integral sums the error and keeps increasing throttle until the error becomes zero.

quiz.q: A host car is set to 30 m/s. The lead car is at 24 m/s and 72 m away. The selected time gap is 2.0 s. Find the time gap, target distance, gap error and closing rate.
quiz.a: t_gap = 72 ÷ 30 = 2.4 s. d_target = 2.0 × 30 = 60 m. e_gap = 72 − 60 = +12 m. Closing rate = 30 − 24 = 6 m/s.

quiz.q: A basic cruise control car speeds up above the set speed on a long downhill. Why can it not correct this?
quiz.a: Basic cruise has throttle authority only. It can close the throttle, but gravity can still push the car faster. Without brake authority it cannot remove the extra speed.

quiz.q: A car cuts in 15 m ahead while ACC is set at 25 m/s with a 2.0 s target gap. Why might ACC fail to avoid a collision?
quiz.a: The cut-in creates a large negative gap error at short range. The needed deceleration may exceed the brake command, and the sensor may not confirm the new target in time. The driver must brake.

quiz.q: What does pressing the brake pedal do to ACC?
quiz.a: It cancels or overrides ACC immediately.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production ACC uses radar and camera fusion, and the gap loop is often model predictive control rather than a simple PI loop. Stop-and-go systems must hold the car on a slope without rolling, so they share work with the electronic parking brake. Search for adaptive cruise control time gap, radar-camera fusion and stop-and-go ACC.
